02 / SELECTED ENGINEERING PROJECTS
Fluid dynamics — experimental research

Flow-regime transition in a Taylor-Couette cell with particle-laden viscoelastic fluids

IMT Nord Europe
Fluid mechanics
CCF vs. EIT — direct visualization of the two flow regimes tracked in this study: laminar Circular Couette Flow (left) and Elasto-Inertial Turbulence (right).
Test rig — Anton-Paar MCR 302 rheometer, cylindrical Taylor-Couette cell, torque measurement on the inner cylinder.
Space-time map — video frames stacked along the cell height (h/δ) reveal exactly where CCF breaks down into EIT as shear increases.

In support of Charles Carré's PhD work, this project characterized non-Newtonian fluids loaded with polymer (HPAM) and particles (PMMA) in a Taylor-Couette flow, to pin down the transition into elasto-inertial turbulence — a chaotic regime of interest for intensifying heat transfer in industrial processes.

The goal was to narrow the particle-concentration window (0–6%) where this transition triggers, by cross-referencing rheometry (torque measured on the rheometer) with direct video visualization (space-time maps built from a MATLAB pipeline).

  • Sample preparation — six HPAM solutions at 300 ppm, from 0 to 5% PMMA, following a protocol adapted from Massoud Moazzen's thesis.
  • Rheometry — Anton-Paar MCR 302, controlled shear ramp, torque acquisition.
  • Video acquisition — DFK33X287 camera at 70 fps; compared AVI vs. MP4 for processing time (3 h vs. 5 min per run).
  • MATLAB processing — frame extraction ("less_frames") and concatenation into a space-time diagram.
  • Cross-correlation — matched the critical Reynolds number read off the space-time map against the slope break in measured torque.
✓

Critical Reynolds number for the CCF→EIT transition located between 4 and 5% PMMA — an optimum-concentration hypothesis, with follow-up needed on sample-to-sample reproducibility.

Spacecraft systems engineering — MBSE

MCURE — a CubeSat mission refining transit ephemerides ahead of ESA's Ariel mission

OSAE — Observatoire de Paris | PSL
Systems engineering
MBSE architecture — functional chain modeled in MATLAB: transit events and pointing feed science coverage, mode, power and data-volume management, all exchanging with the flight software (VTS).
Payload SADT — functional analysis of the optical chain, from light collection to modulation and radio downlink.
Subsystem breakdown — the 3U volume split into three functional units (payload, ADCS, power/telecom), from early sketch to functional diagram.

Ariel (ESA, 2029 launch) must plan its exoplanet transit observations a year ahead, with timing accuracy better than 0.5T. The reference ephemerides date from 2016 and their propagated error grows too large by 2033. MCURE is a 3U CubeSat designed to reconfirm transit mid-times and tighten the orbital-period accuracy for at least 10 high-value targets before Ariel comes online.

I was responsible for structuring and tracing system requirements in a Model-Based Systems Engineering approach (MATLAB), for cross-project coherence (budget, schedule, risk), and for the overall spacecraft design, arbitrating trade-offs between subsystems.

  • Traceability matrix — science requirements broken down to SNR ≥ 5, 10 observed targets, transit-time accuracy < 0.5T.
  • Platform architecture — 3U CubeSat, 30×10×10 cm, 6.35 kg, LEO environment.
  • Orbit selection — sun-synchronous orbit at 600 km, i = 98°, arbitrated by an atmospheric-drag / lifetime trade study.
  • MBSE modeling — science, pointing, intervisibility, coverage, power and data-volume chains modeled end-to-end in MATLAB.
  • Project leadership — €9.8M budget, 7-year schedule, risk matrix and test strategy.
✓

Science coverage validated at 100% across the 10 target stars, after iterating the pointing strategy and orbit choice (Keplerian → sun-synchronous).

Propulsion — electric thrusters / VLEO simulation

Validation of electric-thruster plume and wakefield modelling for Very Low Earth Orbit

Sparc Industries
Electric propulsion · VSTRAP
Figure 11 — Beam and plume characteristics — reference geometry used to frame the plume-current-density analysis and beam divergence study.
Figure 18 — Plume edge extraction — extracting the ion current-density profile at 118 cm from the thruster exit for beam-current integration.
Figure 19 — Ion-beam plume structure — visual reference for the plume geometry used when interpreting the integrated beam current.

Objective. Define and simulate a validation case for plume–wakefield interactions under Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) conditions for electric thrusters, supporting the extension of the VSTRAP simulation platform beyond vacuum-only environments.

The work focused on a QinetiQ T5 / Kaufman-type gridded ion thruster. I first reviewed VLEO electric-propulsion missions and available experimental references, then built a validation workflow in VSTRAP with ParaView post-processing and Python-based extraction of key quantities.

  • Reference definition — selected GOCE's T5 MkV as the representative VLEO case and identified the most usable open experimental data.
  • Plume validation — compared simulated ion current-density profiles against published vacuum measurements at 118 cm from the thruster exit.
  • Single GIO model — moved to a better-documented configuration to validate thrust, grid currents, beam current and erosion-related outputs.
  • Parametric study — tested ETC values of 0.3, 0.4, 0.5 and 0.7 and quantified agreement with the reference data.
  • Post-processing — developed Python scripts to extract grid currents, estimate erosion and integrate the beam current from the plume profile.
✓

Increasing ETC improved agreement for grid currents, thrust and total beam current, while grid-erosion predictions remained poorly reproduced — identifying a clear direction for further model development before full VLEO simulations.

Spacecraft systems — GNC / instrumentation

Low-cost CubeSat attitude determination from two reference vectors

OSAE — Observatoire de Paris | PSL
GNC / instrumentation
Sun vector — Sun–satellite direction derived from solar-panel photocurrent, plotted against the body frame before/after rotation.
Magnetic vector — local magnetic-field direction from the onboard magnetometer, same body-frame convention.
Attitude solution — both vectors realigned on their reference directions by the quaternion rotation, restoring the satellite's attitude live.

Classical attitude-determination hardware (star trackers, gyroscopes) is expensive and out of reach for a small project. The goal was to determine a CubeSat's orientation relative to a reference frame by combining two low-cost measured vectors: the Sun–satellite vector, derived from the photocurrent of 6 solar panels used as directional sensors (I = I₀·cos α), and the magnetic field vector, read from a magnetometer.

Attitude is then computed in quaternions, aligning each measured vector onto its reference, and visualized close to real time.

  • Solar-panel characterization — validated I = I₀·cos(α) under a light source swept across incidence angles.
  • Electronics build — 6 panels + load resistors, magnetometer, ESP32, UART pipeline into a Python buffer/queue for live plotting.
  • Sun vector — computed from the current difference between opposite faces, normalized, and rendered in 3D.
  • Magnetic vector — reference field vector logged on-site via a smartphone app, compared live against the sensor reading.
  • Quaternion rotation — built q = (1 + u·v, u×v) to align each measured vector onto its reference, recovering the satellite's attitude.
✓

Satellite attitude restored close to real time from two low-cost reference vectors, with live 3D Python visualization — running on off-the-shelf Arduino hardware.

Software engineering — Unix pipelines in C

SigGen / WhiteNoiseGen / SigPlot — a modular C toolchain for signal generation and visualization

Master OSAE — Observatoire de Paris | PSL
Software engineering
Reference signal — output of the SigGen → WhiteNoiseGen → SigPlot chain, amplified for display.
Display parameter test — SigPlot's curve-color option validated against the reference trace.
Log-scale test — one of ten integration tests covering SigPlot's display parameters.

Built in a two-person team, this project implements a chain of independent C applications that generate, transform and visualize a digital signal, each communicating strictly through stdin/stdout pipes around a shared, section-based configuration file format:

cat FichierConfig.txt | SigGen | WhiteNoiseGen | SigPlot

Every application reads the full configuration, rewrites only the section it owns, and passes the rest through untouched — a strict contract that made the pipeline's correctness highly dependent on a single shared parser and disciplined error handling on stderr.

  • Shared parser — one parser.c used by all three applications: section detection, parameter conversion, integral pass-through of the configuration, and format-error handling.
  • SigGen — generates a periodic signal (sine, square or triangle) from the requested parameters and writes the samples into the DATA section.
  • WhiteNoiseGen — adds uniform white noise of a given amplitude and seed to the samples already present in DATA.
  • SigPlot — turns the final samples into a Gnuplot script, driving title, axes, color, scale and output format (screen, PNG, PDF, SVG).
  • Test campaign — dedicated test trees per application (valid signals, invalid types, inconsistent parameters) plus ten SigPlot integration tests, each checked against its stdout/stderr pair.
✓

A stable three-stage pipeline (SigGen → WhiteNoiseGen → SigPlot) validated end-to-end, after tracking down pipe-communication bugs — duplicate DATA sections, silent error swallowing — that only surfaced once the applications were chained together.
